messages.text:
"TURBOTREK — MASTER GAME PROMPT

Create an original, fully playable 2D top-down pixel-art arcade racing game called TurboTrek, designed primarily for mobile phones and tablets.

The game should feel like a fun, colorful, classic arcade racer. It should be easy to understand, responsive to touch controls, and enjoyable without realistic driving simulation or complicated physics.

1. Visual style and presentation
Use a consistent, detailed, colorful 2D pixel-art style throughout the entire game.
All cars must be viewed directly from above.
Use original car designs, characters, tracks, icons, animations, music, sound effects, and branding.
Keep the same pixel-art style across the main menu, garage, shop, tracks, HUD, leaderboard, settings, and all other screens.
Do not use realistic 3D graphics, side-view cars, or generic modern mobile-game interfaces.
Use a landscape orientation with a responsive layout for phones and tablets.
Make menus and buttons large enough to use comfortably with touch controls.
Keep the track and cars clearly visible during races.
2. Main menu

Create a pixel-art main menu with these functional options:

Play: Start a regular race.
Tournament: Enter a five-race tournament.
Garage: View, select, and customize cars.
Shop: Purchase cars and cosmetic items using earned tokens.
Settings: Adjust game preferences.

At the first launch, ask the player to enter a racing name. Save the name and display it in races, results, and leaderboards.

3. Racing system

Every regular race must have:

8 cars total: 1 human player and 7 CPU opponents.
3 laps per race.
A randomized starting grid.
A clear finish line and lap detection.
A race timer that starts when the race begins.
A results screen after all racers finish.

The player must be able to steer, accelerate, brake, and drift.

Starting countdown

Before every race, display a large animated pixel-art countdown:

3 → 2 → 1 → START!

Include a checkered flag animation and original countdown sound effect.

All eight cars must remain stationary during the countdown. Neither the player nor CPU opponents may move before START. All cars begin racing at the same time, and the timer starts at START.

Driving and collision
Use simple, responsive arcade-style driving.
Cars must remain within the track boundaries.
Cars must have solid collision detection so they cannot pass through or permanently overlap one another.
Cars should respond naturally when they make contact.
Avoid complicated or overly realistic vehicle physics.
Prevent cars from becoming stuck against track walls or one another.
CPU opponents

Seven CPU racers must participate in every race.

CPU opponents should:

Follow the track correctly.
Maintain reasonable distances from other cars.
Overtake when there is enough room.
Avoid unnecessary contact.
Never intentionally ram, trap, or push the player off the track.
Avoid constantly bumping into other racers.
Finish the race properly, completing all three laps.

Include three difficulty settings:

Easy: Slower opponents, forgiving driving, and wider gaps.
Normal: Balanced speed, handling, and overtaking.
Hard: Faster opponents, better cornering, and smarter overtaking.

Even on Hard, CPU racers must never deliberately ram the player.

4. Racing controls and HUD

Use mobile-friendly touch controls.

During a race, display:

Top-left: Mini-map showing the track and positions of all eight cars.
Top-right: Hamburger menu icon.
Upper screen: Lap counter, current position, and race timer.
Speedometer: Display the player's current speed.
Bottom-left: Virtual joystick for steering.
Bottom-right: Large green accelerate button and large red brake button.

The mini-map must update as the cars move.

Pause menu

Pressing the hamburger icon opens a pause menu with:

Resume Race
Restart Race
Save Game
Settings
Return to Main Menu

The race must pause while this menu is open.

5. Drifting

Add a simple arcade drifting system.

Players can drift around corners.
Drifting should create pixel-art tire marks.
Add small visual effects while drifting.
Successful drifting can earn a small token bonus.
Keep drifting responsive and easy to control.
Prevent unlimited token farming by placing a reasonable limit on drift rewards per race.
6. Cars and abilities

Include 50 original cars, each with a distinct appearance.

Cars should have different combinations of:

Top speed
Acceleration
Handling
Braking

Each car should also have one simple special ability, such as:

Turbo: Temporary speed boost.
Grip Control: Improved handling for a short time.
Quick Start: Better acceleration at the beginning.
Shield: Brief protection from collisions.
Recovery: Faster acceleration after slowing down.
Drift Boost: A small boost after a successful drift.

Abilities must have reasonable cooldowns and must not make one car overwhelmingly powerful.

Car unlocking

Use a combination of progression and token purchases:

Some cars unlock by completing races or reaching milestones.
Other cars can be purchased with earned tokens.
All 50 cars must be obtainable through normal gameplay.
Do not require real-money purchases to unlock cars.

Start the player with a usable car.

7. Garage and customization

Create a functional pixel-art garage.

Players can:

View their unlocked cars.
Select their active racing car.
Compare car statistics.
View each car's special ability.
Customize paint colors.
Add racing stripes.
Change wheel appearance.
Add cosmetic accessories.

Customization should be visual and should not unfairly change vehicle performance.

8. Tracks and maps

Create eight distinct, original, closed-loop racing tracks:

City Streets
Forest Circuit
Desert Raceway
Coastal Highway
Snow Valley
Countryside
Neon Night Circuit
Industrial Raceway

Every track should have its own pixel-art scenery, colors, background details, and atmosphere.

Tracks must have:

Clearly visible road boundaries.
A recognizable starting line and finish line.
Enough room for eight cars to race.
Corners and straight sections.
A corresponding mini-map layout.

Make each track visually different while keeping the racing layout easy to understand.

9. Track conditions and weather

Add changing track conditions, including:

Dry
Wet
Snowy
Cloudy

Weather should initially be mostly visual. Add rain and snow effects where appropriate, without making the game difficult to see or unfair to play.

Include weather controls in Settings:

Weather Effects: ON/OFF
Rain: ON/OFF
Snow: ON/OFF
Cloudy Conditions: ON/OFF

When weather effects are turned off, the corresponding visual effects must stop appearing.

If weather handling effects are implemented, keep them mild and balanced. Do not make weather changes cause unpredictable or uncontrollable driving.

10. Day and night cycle

Include a day/night cycle.

Daytime should have a normal, bright screen.
Nighttime should make the screen noticeably dimmer.
Use subtle pixel-art lighting effects to create a nighttime atmosphere.
Keep the track, cars, road boundaries, and HUD clearly visible at all times.
The lighting can gradually change during a race or between races.

Add a Day/Night Cycle ON/OFF option in Settings.

When disabled, allow the game to remain in normal daytime lighting.

11. Race results and leaderboard

After each race, display all eight racers in their actual finishing order.

The leaderboard must be based on who actually completed the race first, not their starting positions.

Display:

Finishing position.
Racer name.
Race time.
Tokens earned.

Highlight the player's result.

Use:

Gold trophy for first place.
Silver trophy for second place.
Bronze trophy for third place.

Include these buttons:

Race Again
Next Tournament Race
Main Menu

Add a short pixel-art finish-line celebration with a checkered flag and a victory animation for the winner.

12. Token reward system and shop

Create an in-game token currency.

First place receives the largest reward.
Second and third place receive smaller rewards.
Lower finishing positions still receive tokens.
Never take tokens away when the player loses.
Successful drifting can provide a small additional reward.
Display the amount earned after each race.

The Shop should allow players to spend earned tokens on available cars and cosmetic customization items.

Do not include real-money purchases, advertisements, subscriptions, loot boxes, or pay-to-win purchases.

13. Tournament Mode

Tournament Mode must contain exactly five consecutive races.

Each tournament race follows the normal racing format:

Eight cars total.
Three laps.
Seven CPU opponents.

Use a simple tournament points system based on finishing position:

Position	Points
1st	10
2nd	8
3rd	6
4th	5
5th	4
6th	3
7th	2
8th	1

Accumulate points across all five races and display the tournament standings after each race.

After the fifth race, display the final tournament leaderboard.

Tournament rewards
The overall tournament winner receives three times the normal token reward total from the five races.
Formula: Normal five-race token reward total × 3.
The triple reward replaces the normal five-race payouts. It must not be added on top of them.
Players who do not win still receive their normal performance-based rewards.

Display the final tournament winner and their reward clearly.

14. Achievements and player statistics

Add an achievement system with pixel-art achievement icons.

Include achievements such as:

First Victory
Complete 10 Races
Win 5 Tournaments
Set a Personal Best Lap
Finish First on Every Track
Complete Your First Tournament
Successfully Drift During a Race

Display achievement notifications when unlocked.

Track player statistics, including:

Total races.
Total victories.
Podium finishes.
Tournaments completed.
Tournaments won.
Fastest lap.
Best lap time for each track.
15. Personal best and ghost racing

Record the player's best lap time separately for each track.

Where possible, add a ghost racing feature that shows a transparent recording of the player's previous best lap during a new race.

The ghost must not collide with cars or affect the race.

16. Music and sound

Create original retro arcade-style pixel racing music.

Include:

Separate menu and racing music where possible.
Countdown sound effects.
Engine sounds.
Braking and drifting sounds.
Collision sounds.
Achievement notifications.
Victory and results sounds.

Settings must include:

Music ON/OFF.
Music volume control.
Sound Effects ON/OFF.
Sound Effects volume control.

All music and sounds must be original or properly licensed. Do not use copyrighted game music.

17. Save system

The game must preserve player progress after closing and reopening.

Include a manual Save Game option.

Add an Auto Save ON/OFF option in Settings.

Save important information, including:

Player name.
Selected car.
Unlocked cars.
Tokens.
Customization.
Race records.
Achievements.
Player statistics.
Settings and control preferences.
Tournament progress.

Automatically save after completed races, token rewards, purchases, unlocks, and important progress changes when Auto Save is enabled.

18. Quality and implementation requirements

The most important requirement is that the game must actually be playable.

Build the game in stages, in this order:

Stage 1 — Playable racing foundation

One player car.
Seven CPU opponents.
One working track.
Three laps.
Randomized starting grid.
Countdown and simultaneous start.
Steering, acceleration, and braking.
Basic drifting.
Functional collisions and track boundaries.
Working CPU driving.
Mini-map, lap counter, position, timer, and speedometer.
Actual race results and finishing order.
Basic token rewards.

Stage 2 — Main game systems

Main menu and garage.
Player name.
Save system.
Difficulty settings.
Car statistics and abilities.
Shop and car unlocking.
Tournament Mode.
Achievements and player statistics.

Stage 3 — Content and visual features

All eight tracks.
All 50 cars.
Car customization.
Weather and track conditions.
Day/night cycle.
Music and sound controls.
Ghost racing and additional visual effects.

Prioritize stable, working gameplay over decorative menus or large amounts of content.

Do not create buttons that do nothing. Do not display fake race results, fake lap counters, or fake AI positions. Every feature shown to the player must work.

If a feature cannot be implemented reliably yet, leave it out of the playable build until it can be implemented correctly rather than pretending it works.

Keep the code and game systems organized so additional cars, tracks, abilities, and features can be added without breaking the racing foundation.

FINAL GOAL: Deliver an original, colorful, fully playable top-down pixel-art arcade racer called TurboTrek, with responsive controls, fair CPU opponents, satisfying drifting, varied tracks, car progression, customization, and replay value. The game should be fun to play first and expanded with additional content without sacrificing stability.

---
This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.

Screenshots for your own checks: save small JPEGs (a .jpg path, viewport at most 1280px wide) and read only the latest one; older images are dropped from context. Read a full-size PNG only when fine detail matters.
"

1: ## Process lifecycle
2: 
3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.
6: 
7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

Built **TurboTrek** as a self-contained browser game in `index.html`, `style.css`, and `game.js`.

The current build includes a pixel-inspired racing screen, name entry, keyboard and touch controls, a countdown, seven CPU racers, a minimap, lap/position/time/speed HUD, three-lap races, results, token rewards, settings, and local save data.

**Run it:** serve the project directory with a local web server and open `index.html`. I verified `game.js` parses with `node --check`.

This is a playable foundation, not the full master spec: features such as tournament mode, the full garage/shop, 50 cars, and all eight distinct tracks remain to be implemented.
